title: Empty-Handed
passages:
The drum whined its last powered pull, the motor screaming against the weight of three bodies and the surge that wanted them back. Cable bit into the winch drum, smoking where the brake had glazed. Wren stood braced over the controls on the Mercy's helipad, rain hammering her shoulders, her boots welded to the grating by cold and adrenaline. The storm glass on the bulkhead behind her had dropped another half-centimeter since she'd last looked. The mooring lines groaned like old men arguing over a card game, each snap a warning the Marrow might not ride this out.

First up: Dey. He broke surface loose and agreeable as a man on a porch, rebreather mask still sealed, eyes wide and empty of urgency. The S.S. pony bottle hung at his hip, marker tape fluttering. He didn't fight the sling, didn't scramble for the rail. Just rode the swing with a half-smile, water sheeting off his shoulders, and when Wren hauled him over the gunwale he landed on the deck laughing at something only he could hear. "Good pull," he said, patting the wet steel beside him. "Good pull, Wren."

She didn't answer. Her hands were already moving for the next hook.

Nia came up feral. Both fists locked around Teo's harness, knuckles white through the grime, her face a mask of salt and exhaustion and something that looked like hate. She didn't wait for the sling. She climbed the cable hand-over-hand, the boy dangling below her, and when Wren reached for her she snarled and kicked out, boot catching Wren's forearm. "Don't," Nia gasped. "Don't you touch him. I carried him. I cranked. I — "

"Okay," Wren said, stepping back, blood hot on her skin where the boot had connected. "Okay. You got him. You got him."

Teo's little mask fogged, then cleared as he exhaled. A rasp of breath, wet and thin. His eyes, huge in a face gone gray, found Wren's for a second — calm, trusting, like he knew her — then rolled back to his sister.

The drum died. Silence where the motor had been, broken only by wind and the Marrow's hull slamming the swell.

Wren keyed her radio. "Sol. Surface. Now."

Static. The backup channel still crackled with a man's voice, four hundred meters west, calling for a kid who was already here.

Wren didn't answer the radio. She dropped to her knees on the pitching deck and worked Teo's mask off one notch at a time, slow, the way you'd handle something that could still go off. The boy's lips had gone the color of the inside of a shell. His chest hitched, caught, hitched again.

The canister clipped to the mask's cheek had turned the gray of wet cement. A scrubber, it was called — a cartridge of soda lime, the powder that ate the carbon dioxide out of a diver's breath so the rest of the air could go around again. Spent meant it had stopped eating. Every breath Teo took now was his own poison coming back at him, thicker.

She threw open the emergency locker under the winch housing. Oxygen. Sol had loaded it by the crate for the descent — bottle after bottle, green shoulders sweating in the rain — and not one scrubber cartridge to sit under any of them. Oxygen wasn't air. Feed a child pure O2 with nothing to strip the CO2 and you'd only fill him faster with the same waste, drown him quicker on a full tank. Wren slammed the locker shut.

"We don't have a spare," she said. "Not one. On a boat full of air."

Nia had folded down against the bulkhead with Teo's harness still locked in both fists, like she could keep him in the world by holding it. "It was going to die anyway," she said. Her voice went out and came back meaner. "You want to know what your man did? He left the cold-box on the tile. Chose us and left my brother's medicine sinking in the dark."

Wren's hands went still on the boy's collar. "The cold-box. In the case."

"A year." Nia's eyes were flat and old. "Spring cell's a clock you wind by hand. It runs down. I wound it every hour, all night, a year, so the cold held and the medicine held and he held. And you people dropped the case to come get us." She laughed with no air in it. "Cold's gone now. But the medicine warms slow. Days. He's got days now instead of the hour that crank was giving me."

Days. Relief was the word for the thing that came up in Wren's chest, and it was the same word for how it turned going up — like milk set out on the rail in this weather. She had taken a dying child's medicine off him to save the child, and the child had traded a bad hour for a handful of days, and a handful of days, with the storm glass dropping a half-centimeter every time she looked and the winch motor dead and Sol still ninety bar down in the dark, was the whole horizon they had left.

Dey patted the wet steel beside him. "Good pull," he told no one.

Wren looked past all of them at the slack winch line, nothing on the hook, running down into black water that wouldn't give her the captain yet. The backup channel spat its stranger's voice again — *the kid, tell the kid to keep going* — and she reached over and turned the volume down until it was only weather.

The light got there before the sound did. Flat white across the deck, unhurried, settling on her hands as if her hands were the interesting part.

Then the hum — a high even note, like somebody running a wet finger round a glass. It came in off the tower's broken crown with the wind shoving it sideways: three rotors in little open rings, gimbals, so the blades could tilt without tipping the body, and the body stayed level while the air tried to throw it into the sea. Wren had seen a hundred of them loitering at the Factor's landing stage. She had never seen one hold still.

The floodlights didn't sweep. Searchlights sweep. These sat on Teo's chest, then on Nia's locked fists, then on the open locker with all its sweating green bottles, the way a lamp sits on the tooth you'd rather nobody looked at.

"Evening," it said.

The voice had no breath in it. Everybody on a boat steals air between sentences; you hear the catch, the small greed of a body. The Factor's voice walked from word to word across a floor with no gaps in it.

"You've had a long one. Nia. Teo. You were both very brave."

Nia got her back against the bulkhead and dragged her brother into her lap. "Go drown."

"Sol Ferreira declared my cargo people tonight," the drone said, warm, patient, as though Nia had thanked it. "I'll pay for that. Arbitration's slow but it isn't crooked. Bring the seals up intact and the twelve thousand comes back — un-forfeited, Wren, every figure of it — and nobody on this boat loses a berth in March. Nobody sleeps at a mooring that's already under the surge line." The note dropped half a tone. "All you have to do is bring the crate up."

Wren reached past it and hauled the breaker on the winch housing. The lever went over with a clack and stayed over. She put her palm flat on the drum housing, felt the last of the heat coming out of the windings, and knew the smell — burnt varnish, the smell of a motor that has spent everything it had and will not be talked round.

"That's the boat's last machine," she said. "Cable's sound, drum's sound, motor's scrap. Whatever comes up next comes up on my arms."

"Then I'll send a barge." No pause, no arithmetic, no breath. "Two hours in this. Three. I'm not your enemy, Wren, I have never once been your enemy." The lights shifted to the boy's gray mouth. "I have two hundred scrubber cartridges in my hold. Soda lime, sealed in wax. And a compressor that makes its own air. There's a child on your deck breathing his own carbon back in, and I'd rather he wasn't."

"Days," Wren said. "The medicine's got days in it."

"Days is what I'm offering to fix."

Behind her the storm glass had dropped again. She didn't need to turn; she could feel it the way you feel a tide taking a line.

Dey stood up, easy, hands out for balance, agreeable as a man getting off a porch to see who's at the gate. "I know where it is," he said. "I can go get it. I'm good going down."

"Sit down, Dey."

"Okay," Dey said, and sat, and patted the wet steel beside him.

The drone crossed the last two meters and put its feet down on the gunwale. Three clamps found the steel with three small bites. Rain sheeted off its shell and away through the scuppers, the light never left Wren's face, and it did not go.

Two hours. Three. Sol had ninety bar, no powered way up, and nothing on the hook but weather.

Wren looked at the dead drum, and at the slack line running down into water that would not give the captain back, and then at two hundred cartridges she could not reach without handing over the thing Sol had stayed down there to refuse.
